# Rob Mitchell — auction context and trading with value

Primary source: [Rob Mitchell webinar, olGRYb_xtwQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ), introduced by Big Mike as auction-market theory and trading with value. This is Mitchell's teaching curated through Vern's selected material. The host's questions and introductory brokerage presentation have separate authorship; neither becomes Vern's personal trading record.

**Exact coverage:** complete English auto-generated transcript read, **00:02–1:51:36**, all **2,640 lines**. Retained `transcripts/olGRYb_xtwQ.txt`: 119,945 bytes, SHA-256 `b795b7aac6e3478ad7d4ae0051aaca5602098dfe5393b611854389f4a82e947f`. No audio verification or video chart-frame inspection was performed for this note. ASR mistakes and uncertain recalled numbers limit precision. The opening brokerage discussion was read but is historical promotional context, not evaluated as a present service recommendation.

## His central distinction: advertised price versus accepted value

Mitchell starts with an art-auction analogy ([18:33–26:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=1113s)). Price moves while testing willingness to transact; the concentration of actual transactions is his operational proxy for accepted value. A volume profile organizes those transactions by price rather than merely displaying the last quoted/traded price.

He describes the POC as the largest volume concentration in the chosen interval and uses a value area containing 70% of trading ([29:56–34:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=1796s)). High-volume regions tend to attract/congest price in his account; low-volume regions offer less stopping power once traversed. He seeks breakouts with room to travel into low participation rather than an entry immediately facing another congested area.

**Abacus qualification:** the analogy helps explain the distinction but is not a statistical market model. The fifty-person painting example's 98% is an arithmetic detail of that fictional audience, not a measured trading probability. Repeated transactions also cannot identify a unique count of investors agreeing on fundamental value.

## Opening location starts a hypothesis

At [36:14–45:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=2174s), his preparation uses opening location, prior value/range, composite volume and scheduled news. His textbook examples are:

| Opening situation | His initial expectation | What still has to be observed |
|---|---|---|
| Inside prior value | More rotation/ranging | Whether new information changes the auction |
| Above prior value | Bullish bias; consider buying a retracement | Whether the market holds/accepts the higher context |
| Below prior value | Bearish bias; consider selling a retracement | Whether the lower auction persists |
| Beyond the prior range as well | Stronger initial change in perceived value | Whether the break actually follows through |

He explicitly calls these basic scenarios and acknowledges failures. The timing and market reaction to a report matter even when he does not try to predict its content. At [1:33:20–1:37:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=5600s), he describes a contrary example: an above-value opening followed by a negative report, re-entry through value and a selloff. His response relies on judgment; this discussion does not supply a complete mechanical failure detector.

## Shape describes a process, not a guaranteed outcome

At [47:01–56:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=2821s), he uses four familiar shapes:

- **D:** a central distribution associated with balance; a departure asks whether accepted value has changed.
- **Small b:** a decline followed by consolidation, associated in his explanation with liquidation.
- **P:** a rally followed by consolidation, associated with covering.
- **Capital B:** separated distributions, associated in his explanation with continuation.

He further reduces the picture into distributions and the movements connecting them. A gap may omit a visible stem; a directional day may contain several internal distributions. That is useful for reading development without requiring a perfect letter shape.

He also says that new participation must sustain an initial covering/liquidation move if it is to persist. **Our boundary:** shape alone does not identify which transactions opened new positions or closed old ones. The covering/liquidation story remains an interpretation unless separate position evidence supports it. Likewise a thin volume profile and a TPO single print are different measurements even though his language sometimes groups them together.

## Composite context and execution operate on different horizons

At [56:17–1:03:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=3377s), he compares value areas across days, their width/overlap and the position of low/high volume on composites. He keeps the larger picture visible to avoid overtrading a tiny intraday range.

In Q&A at [1:09:10–1:15:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=4150s), he loosely anchors composites to at least one market cycle rather than a universal number of days. He uses day data for his then-primary Russell market; his prior ES practice included overnight views. He and the host discuss the difficulties of old contracts and back-adjustment, without establishing one correct construction. Their chart settings are historical configurations.

At [1:17:05–1:22:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=4625s), a break above a compact multisession balance leads him to an initial trend bias, with volume needed to support the move. This is a correction to automatically fading every apparent extreme. At [1:27:01–1:29:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=5221s), he differentiates a prior POC as an inside-value magnet from its potential reaction role after an outside-value opening.

Crucially, at [1:25:23–1:26:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=5123s), he distinguishes these larger profile scenarios from **his own short-duration breakout execution**. Profile analysis frames the direction and space; the exact personal entry comes from his shorter chart work. His historical Russell stop size and scale-outs at [1:38:05–1:42:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=5885s) should not be transplanted into ES or attributed to Vern.

## Where the sources differ

Mitchell considers retracements to a **prior** VAH/VAL or POC in his textbook opening scenarios ([41:48–42:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=2508s)). Hoffman and Kumar's [value-transition discussion](video-value-transition.md) warns against entering at the **current accepted mode solely because it is POC**. These are distinct uses of a level. The knowledge base therefore cannot state either “always trade POC” or “never trade POC” as the combined doctrine.

Mitchell's quick scale-out/breakeven preference also belongs to his personal execution style. It does not settle Dalton's objection to arbitrary stop placement or override Vern's setup-specific management examples.

## Analytical cautions and unresolved evidence

- **70% coverage is a setting, not proof of normality.** His sigma percentages at [30:54–31:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=1854s) are imprecise. Do not infer Gaussian tail odds from a profile or equate any visually D-shaped histogram with a demonstrated normal distribution.
- **The 80% rule is not validated here.** At [1:37:03–1:37:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=olGRYb_xtwQ&t=5823s), the host recalls the rule uncertainly and Mitchell says he has not run that test. Their agreement is not independent evidence for Vern's reported statistic.
- **Low volume supports competing paths.** Rejection from a low-participation boundary and rapid travel through it depend on response and context. A node label alone cannot choose between them.
- **The personal “zero risk” description is informal.** Moving a stop toward entry after a partial exit does not itself demonstrate zero possible loss after execution costs and adverse fills. No complete fill record is supplied.
- **Method and results remain separate.** The transcript contains selected chart examples, intuitive decisions and asserted tendencies. It supplies no reproducible dataset, event definitions, uncertainty estimates or out-of-sample performance record.

The practical abstraction is to prepare an opening hypothesis, identify the next accepted/rejected areas and available travel space, then compare live action with that hypothesis. The hypothesis must be revisable. Exact triggers, acceptance duration, composite anchors, stop logic and expected outcomes remain separate research specifications.
